text.text: A ten-minute tour for every bookseller. Read it once; the rhythm at the end is the week.

: copies going back, why, and the credit you are owed.

Replace the sample publishers and titles with your own stock, then your regulars. Delete the sample orders once real ones come in. Customers' reading notes are for recommending books, nothing else.
Sales, special orders, stock and events at a glance.
Special orders are how an independent bookstore beats the internet: any book, a person who remembers your name, and a call when it arrives.
Look the title up with the distributor. Check it is in print and when it can arrive.
: customer, title, copies, deposit. Tell the customer the expected date, honestly.
Take a deposit: 10 dollars for one book, about a third for class sets and book club orders. Write it in
Add it to the next distributor order (Monday and Thursday).

Book clubs order ten or more copies a few weeks ahead; teachers order class sets. Give them 10 percent off and confirm the count in writing a week before you order. Ask the teacher for a purchase order number if the school pays.
Check the box against the order. Match each book to its slip.
. Put the book behind the counter with the slip in it, spine out, by last name.

If you cannot reach them, try again in three days, and once more by email.
Hold special orders for 14 days after the call.
When the customer collects, take the balance and press
Uncollected after 14 days and two reminders: the deposit is kept, the book goes on the shelf or back to the publisher.

If the distributor reports a book out of stock or out of print, call the customer the same day with the choice: wait, a different edition, a used copy from a trusted source, or a refund of the deposit. Never let a special order go quiet.
: orders past their expected date and books that have arrived but not been collected. Each line is a customer waiting on you or a book taking up shelf space.
Most new books can go back to the publisher for credit. Using returns well keeps the shelves fresh and the cash moving.

A book that has not sold in four to six months is taking the place of one that would. Publishers expect returns within their window and give credit against future orders. Booksellers who never return books end up with shelves of stock nobody wants and no room for the new season.
On the first Monday of the month, sort
by publication date and copies sold.
Pull hardcovers more than six months out with few or no sales, paperbacks more than nine months, and frontlist that did not take off.
Keep staff picks, local interest and anything with a book club or school coming.
for each title: copies, reason, the publisher, and the credit (copies x your cost).
Some distributors need you to request authorization; others take returns within their window without asking. Check the terms on the publisher's row. When authorized, set
and write the authorization number in the notes.
Pack tightly so books do not shift; damaged returns are refused.
Put the authorization and a packing list inside.
Ship by the cheapest tracked method; keep the receipt.
and take the copies off the shelf count.
to about 30 days after shipping. Check the statement each month; when the credit appears, set
. Credit that has not appeared by its date needs a polite email to the publisher's accounts team.

Local authors on consignment are not returned for credit: their unsold copies go back to the author after the agreed time. Sidelines (book lights, cards) are usually not returnable; buy them carefully.
Events need stock on hand, so order generously and return what is left within the window. Keep a few signed copies; signed books sell over the following weeks.
A good event fills the shop, sells books on the night and for weeks after, and makes the store part of its neighbourhood.

Pick a host from the team and decide the format: reading and signing, a conversation with a local guest, a story time, or an offsite venue for a bigger name.
Count seats. The shop holds 60 with the tables moved.
Order stock: one copy for about two-thirds of the seats for an established author, half for a debut. Place it as

current. Above the seat count, think about a bigger room.

Start on time. The host introduces the author in under two minutes. Reading and conversation run about 40 minutes, then questions, then the signing. Sell before and after; ring each sale as channel
so you know what the night was worth.
Keep a stack of signed copies for the front table.
Return unsold unsigned stock within the publisher's window.
Send the author or publicist a thank-you with the numbers.
is the one to watch: about half a copy per seat is solid for a debut; above one is a great night. Events that sell little but bring new faces still earn their place; note who came for the first time.
